etymology: From the cloven tongues "like as of fire" that sat upon the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 2:3); fire from Old English fýr, a common biblical emblem of God's purifying, illuminating, and consuming presence.
biblical_def: The Fire of the Spirit is a scriptural figure for the Holy Ghost's purifying, illuminating, and zeal-kindling work, drawn chiefly from Pentecost, where there appeared unto the disciples "cloven tongues like as of fire," and it sat upon each of them (Acts 2:3). John the Baptist had foretold that the Messiah would baptize "with the Holy Ghost, and with fire" (Matt 3:11). The figure must be read by the analogy of faith, not by enthusiasm. Fire in Scripture signifies several settled realities of the Spirit's ministry. First, purification: as the refiner's fire purges dross from silver, so the Spirit sanctifies the saints, burning away corruption and conforming them to Christ. Second, illumination: fire gives light, and the Spirit enlightens the understanding to behold the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ as that glory shines forth from the written word. Third, zeal: the disciples were set ablaze for the proclamation of the gospel, their hearts burning within them. The apostolic charge therefore runs, "Quench not the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19)—a man may, by sloth, neglect, or cherished sin, damp and stifle the Spirit's gracious operations as water quenches a flame. Yet this fire is not raw emotionalism, nor the manufactured frenzy of the revival-bench, nor a fresh revelation added to the closed canon. The Spirit's fire always burns along the channel of the word He Himself inspired; He kindles holy affections toward the truths of Scripture, never apart from them. To seek the "fire" as an experience detached from the word and the means of grace is to chase a strange fire the Lord hath not commanded. This dictionary confesses the Spirit's fire as the heart-warming, sin-purging, word-illuminating zeal of God in His people, ever subject to and proved by the sufficient and closed Scriptures.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 treats FIRE as the effect of combustion, giving heat and light, and figuratively as ardor of affection or zeal. The Fire of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's purifying, illuminating, and zeal-kindling work, emblematized in the Pentecostal tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).
webster_full: FIRE, n. — The effect of combustion. The combustion of inflammable substances, producing heat and light. Figuratively, ardor of affection; the heat or warmth of zeal or animation.

In the spiritual sense, the Fire of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's sanctifying and illuminating presence, appearing at Pentecost as cloven tongues "like as of fire" resting upon the disciples (Acts 2:3).
"And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them" (Acts 2:3).
The figure requires the purging of dross, the giving of light to the understanding, and the kindling of holy zeal—and forbids the quenching of the Spirit by sloth or cherished sin (1 Thess 5:19).
It is no warrant for emotionalism or fresh revelation, but the heart-warming zeal of God exercised always along the channel of His written and sufficient word.
scriptures: And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them.
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.
And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
corruption_summary: The Fire of the Spirit is corrupted when it is reduced to worked-up emotionalism or claimed as a fresh, canon-supplementing revelation, both of which detach the Spirit's work from the word He inspired.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief abuse of this figure is the substitution of emotional heat for the Spirit's genuine work. Whole movements have taught the saints to seek "the fire" as a felt experience—a quickened pulse, a flood of feeling, a frenzy at the altar—treating the intensity of the sensation as the measure of the Spirit's presence. But Scripture nowhere makes feeling the test of the Spirit; it makes the word the test of feeling. The Spirit's fire purifies from sin and conforms to Christ; where there is much heat and little holiness, the fire is strange and not from heaven. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire which the Lord commanded not, and were consumed. The remedy is to seek the Spirit at the means He has appointed—the preached and read word, the sacraments, prayer—and to test every supposed kindling by the fruit of the Spirit and the doctrine of Scripture.

A second corruption claims the Spirit's fire as a fresh outpouring that adds new revelation to the church, as though the canon were still open and God were yet speaking words to be received with the authority of Scripture. This dictionary is cessationist: the Spirit no longer gives new inspired words, for the faith was once delivered unto the saints and the Scriptures are complete and sufficient. The fire that burns in true believers is the same Spirit applying the same finished word to the heart, making the saints' hearts burn within them as the Scriptures are opened (Luke 24:32). To recover the doctrine is to seek a holy, word-fed zeal—not visions, prophecies, or revelations, but a heart set aflame with love to the God who has already spoken fully in His Son and in the closed canon.
roots_summary: The figure rests on the Pentecostal tongues of fire (Acts 2:3) and the Old Testament emblem of fire as God's purifying and illuminating presence, behind the Greek pyr and the Hebrew esh.
roots_lines: Greek pyr (G4442) — fire; the element of the Pentecostal tongues and a frequent emblem of divine presence and judgment.
Hebrew 'esh (H784) — fire; the pillar of fire, the burning bush, the refiner's fire of God's purifying dealings.
Greek zēlos (G2205) — zeal, fervor; the holy ardor the Spirit kindles in the saints toward God and His truth.
Greek sbennymi (G4570) — to quench, extinguish; the verb of 1 Thess 5:19, warning against stifling the Spirit's operations.
The figure is always governed by the word: the Spirit's fire burns along the channel of the Scripture He inspired, never apart from it.
usage: The preacher prayed that the Fire of the Spirit would purge his own dross before he dared to handle the word in the pulpit.
What passed for the Fire of the Spirit at the meeting was mere emotional heat, untested by Scripture and barren of holiness.
"Quench not the Spirit"—the saint is charged not to damp the Fire of the Spirit by sloth or cherished sin.

etymology: From Greek baptizō, to dip, immerse, overwhelm; the phrase rendering Paul's "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body" (1 Cor 12:13), the Spirit's uniting of every believer to Christ at conversion.
biblical_def: The Baptism of the Spirit is the saving work whereby the Holy Ghost unites every believer to Christ and incorporates him into the one body, the church, at the moment of conversion. The locus classicus is Paul's declaration, "For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit" (1 Cor 12:13). The grammar is decisive: all are baptized, not a favored few; it is the common possession of the whole church, not a higher tier of advanced saints. John the Baptist foretold that Christ would baptize with the Holy Ghost (Mark 1:8), and at Pentecost this promise was first poured out upon the church; thereafter every one who is savingly joined to Christ partakes of the same Spirit. To be baptized with the Spirit is therefore the same reality as being regenerated, indwelt, and united to Christ—it is conversion viewed from the side of the Spirit's incorporating work, not a distinct experience subsequent to and higher than faith. Against this the Pentecostal and charismatic movements teach a "second blessing," a baptism in the Spirit received some time after conversion and evidenced by speaking in tongues, dividing the church into Spirit-baptized haves and merely-converted have-nots. This dictionary rejects that scheme as contrary to the plain sense of 1 Corinthians 12:13. Every believer already has the Spirit; if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His (Rom 8:9). The saints are exhorted, not to seek a second baptism, but to be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18)—an ongoing, repeated yielding to His government, distinct from the once-for-all baptism that incorporates. This dictionary confesses one Spirit-baptism, common to all the redeemed, received at conversion, the bond of the church's unity.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BAPTISM as the application of water as a religious rite, and figuratively an overwhelming or initiation. The Baptism of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's uniting of every believer to Christ and His body at conversion (1 Cor 12:13).
webster_full: BAPTISM, n. — The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ. Figuratively, an overwhelming, an immersing, an initiation.
In the spiritual sense, the Baptism of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's once-for-all incorporation of the believer into the body of Christ at conversion.
"For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body... and have been all made to drink into one Spirit" (1 Cor 12:13).
It requires that we regard the Spirit's baptism as common to all believers; it forbids the doctrine of a second blessing reserved for an elite and evidenced by tongues.
It is to be distinguished from the repeated command to be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18), which is the ongoing yielding of the saint to the Spirit's government.
scriptures: For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.
I indeed have baptized you with water: but he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost.
But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.
corruption_summary: The Baptism of the Spirit is corrupted by the Pentecostal second-blessing doctrine, which makes it a post-conversion experience evidenced by tongues and divides the church into two classes of Christians.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pentecostal and charismatic movements teach that the baptism of the Spirit is a distinct experience subsequent to conversion, to be sought and received by the already-converted, and authenticated by the initial physical evidence of speaking in tongues. On this scheme the church is divided into two tiers: ordinary believers who have been saved, and Spirit-baptized believers who have received the higher endowment. But Paul says all are baptized by one Spirit into one body (1 Cor 12:13), and lists the gifts, tongues included, as distributed severally as the Spirit wills, not as the universal mark of a second blessing—"do all speak with tongues?" he asks, expecting the answer No. The doctrine breeds spiritual pride in those who claim the experience and a crippling sense of second-rate discipleship in those who do not. The remedy is to see that every believer, at conversion, already possesses the indwelling Spirit and is already a full member of Christ's body.

Being cessationist, this dictionary further denies that the sign-gift of tongues continues as a normative endowment for the church today; the apostolic sign-gifts attended the foundation-laying era and have ceased with the completion of the canon. The recovery of the doctrine is therefore twofold. First, against the two-tier scheme, confess one baptism common to all the saved, so that no believer is taught to seek what he already has or to despise himself for lacking what God never made the badge of true faith. Second, redirect the saint's pursuit from a sought-after crisis experience to the lifelong, repeated command to be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18)—walking in the Spirit, mortifying the deeds of the body, yielding daily to the Spirit's government through the word and the means of grace.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on Paul's en heni pneumati... ebaptisthemen (1 Cor 12:13), the once-for-all baptism by the one Spirit into the one body, distinguished from the ongoing filling of Ephesians 5:18.
roots_lines: Greek baptizō (G907) — to dip, immerse, overwhelm; the verb of the Spirit's incorporating act in 1 Cor 12:13.
Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit; the one Spirit who baptizes all the saved into the one body of Christ.
Greek sōma (G4983) — body; the church into which every believer is baptized by the Spirit.
Greek plēroō (G4137) — to fill; the verb of Eph 5:18, the repeated yielding distinct from the once-for-all baptism.
The aorist of 1 Cor 12:13 marks a completed act true of every believer at conversion, not a recurring or elite experience.
usage: Because all are baptized by one Spirit into one body, the Baptism of the Spirit is the bond of the whole church, not the badge of a few.
He had been taught to seek the Baptism of the Spirit as a second blessing, until he saw that 1 Corinthians 12:13 made it the common gift of every believer at conversion.
The pastor distinguished the once-for-all Baptism of the Spirit from the daily command to be filled with the Spirit.

etymology: From Greek symmartyreō, to bear witness together with; the phrase rendering Paul's "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Rom 8:16).
biblical_def: The Witness of the Spirit is the gracious work of the Holy Ghost whereby He confirms to the believer's own consciousness that he is indeed a child of God, and so undergirds the assurance of salvation. The foundation text is Romans 8:16: "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." The verb is symmartyreō, to witness together with: the Spirit does not testify in a vacuum, nor merely to us, but bears witness with our spirit, joining His testimony to the renewed conscience of the believer. Two witnesses thus concur—the Spirit and the saint's own spirit—and in the mouth of two witnesses the matter is established. This witness operates chiefly by enabling the believer to cry, "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6), shedding abroad the love of God in the heart and giving a filial confidence toward God. It is crucial to mark what this witness is not. It is no fresh revelation, no audible voice, no new word added to Scripture telling the man his name is written in the book of life. This dictionary is cessationist: the Spirit gives no new inspired words. Rather, the Spirit's witness works through and by the word already given, applying its promises and its marks of grace to the heart, illuminating the evidences of regeneration that the word itself describes—love of the brethren, hatred of sin, delight in God's law, the keeping of His commandments—so that the believer, examining himself by Scripture and feeling the Spirit's seal upon the verdict, is assured. Assurance therefore rests on a threefold cord: the promises of the word, the fruits of grace in the life, and the witness of the Spirit confirming both. This dictionary confesses that the Spirit's witness is a real, sweet, and solid ground of assurance—not a mystical bypass of the word, but the Spirit's own amen, set upon His own written promises, in the heart of His own child.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WITNESS as testimony, attestation of a fact, and one who gives evidence. The Witness of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's confirming testimony, joined to the believer's renewed spirit, that he is a child of God (Rom 8:16).
webster_full: WITNESS, n. — Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. Also, one who knows or sees any thing; one personally present; one who gives testimony or evidence.
In the spiritual sense, the Witness of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost bearing witness together with the believer's spirit that he is a child of God.
"The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Rom 8:16).
It requires that the saint ground assurance on the Spirit's confirming testimony joined to the word and the fruits of grace; it forbids resting on a fresh revelation or inward voice.
It is no new word added to Scripture, but the Spirit's amen set upon His own written promises in the heart of His child.
scriptures: The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.
For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit.
corruption_summary: The Witness of the Spirit is corrupted when it is treated as a fresh private revelation or an inward voice giving new information, rather than the Spirit's confirming testimony exercised through the closed and sufficient word.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common abuse turns the witness of the Spirit into a species of private revelation—an impression, an inward voice, a sudden conviction that descends upon the mind announcing "you are saved," received with the same authority as Scripture and beyond all examination. On this view assurance floats free of the word and of the fruits of grace, resting wholly on the strength of a feeling, so that a man may presume upon a comfortable impression while his life gives no evidence of regeneration. But Scripture knows no such bare witness. The Spirit bears witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16), joining His testimony to the renewed conscience as it judges the life by the marks of grace the word lays down; and John gives the test plainly: "hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments" (1 John 2:3). A witness that cannot bear the trial of the word and the life is no witness of the Holy Ghost.

Because this dictionary is cessationist, it denies that the Spirit's witness is any new inspired communication. The canon is closed; the Spirit speaks no fresh words. His witness is the application of the word already given—sealing the promises, illuminating the evidences, shedding abroad the love of God in the heart so that the believer cries Abba, Father with filial confidence. The recovery of the doctrine is to set the witness of the Spirit upon its proper foundation: the threefold cord of the promises of Scripture, the fruits of grace tried by self-examination, and the Spirit's confirming seal. So grounded, assurance is no presumption and no mysticism, but the solid joy of a child of God who has the Spirit's own amen upon the verdict of the word.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on Paul's to pneuma symmartyrei tōi pneumati hēmōn (Rom 8:16), the Spirit witnessing together with the believer's spirit, and the filial cry "Abba, Father."
roots_lines: Greek symmartyreō (G4828) — to bear witness together with; the verb of Rom 8:16, the Spirit testifying with our spirit.
Greek martyria (G3141) — witness, testimony; the legal-forensic background of two concurring witnesses establishing a matter.
Aramaic abba (G5) — father; the intimate filial address the Spirit of adoption enables (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6).
Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; the settled confidence the Spirit's witness produces in the heart.
The witness is no new revelation but the Spirit's confirming seal applied through the already-given and sufficient word.
usage: When his conscience accused him, the Witness of the Spirit, joined to the promises of the word, assured him he was a child of God.
The Witness of the Spirit is no inward voice with fresh information, but the Spirit's amen set upon Scripture in the believer's heart.
Assurance rests on a threefold cord—the promises, the fruits of grace, and the Witness of the Spirit confirming both.

etymology: From Latin convincere, to overcome, prove guilty; the sense rendering the Greek elenchō, to reprove or convince, in Christ's promise that the Comforter would "reprove the world of sin" (John 16:8).
biblical_def: Conviction of Sin is the work of the Holy Ghost whereby He so applies the law and the gospel to a man's conscience that he is brought to see, feel, and own his guilt before a holy God. The Lord Jesus promised this ministry: "And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment" (John 16:8). The verb is elenchō, to convict as a court convicts the guilty—not merely to inform of sin in the abstract, but to fasten guilt upon the conscience so that the sinner cannot evade the verdict. This conviction has both a preparatory and an ongoing aspect. Preparatory, it is that work by which the Spirit, often through the preached law, slays the sinner's self-righteousness, stops his mouth, and shows him guilty before God (Rom 3:19), so that, despairing of himself, he flees to Christ. Such was Peter's congregation at Pentecost, who, hearing the word, were "pricked in their heart, and said... Men and brethren, what shall we do?" (Acts 2:37). Ongoing, conviction continues in the believer, the Spirit using the word to humble him under remaining sin, to keep him tender of conscience, and to drive him afresh to the blood of Christ for cleansing. It is therefore the Spirit's instrument against all easy-believism, which would have men profess faith without ever feeling the weight of their sin or the need of a Savior. A gospel that never convicts has never converted. Yet conviction is not its own end and must not be confused with saving faith; it is the Spirit's plough breaking up the fallow ground, that the seed of the gospel may take root, and it always aims beyond itself at Christ. This dictionary confesses conviction of sin as a true and necessary work of the Spirit, humbling the sinner and the saint alike, and ever driving the convicted soul not to despair but to the cross.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONVICTION as the act of convincing of sin; the state of being convinced or convicted by conscience; the act of compelling one to admit the truth. Conviction of Sin is the Spirit's reproving work fastening guilt upon the conscience (John 16:8).
webster_full: CONVICTION, n. — 1. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge. 2. In law, the act of finding a person guilty. 3. The act of convincing of sin, or the state of being convinced; the state of the conscience under a sense of guilt.
In the spiritual sense, Conviction of Sin is the Holy Ghost's work of reproving the conscience so that the sinner sees, feels, and owns his guilt before God.
"And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment" (John 16:8).
It requires the Spirit to slay self-righteousness and drive the sinner to Christ; it forbids the easy-believism that professes faith without any sense of sin.
It is the plough breaking the fallow ground, never an end in itself, but always aiming beyond itself at the cross of Christ.
scriptures: And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment.
Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
corruption_summary: Conviction of Sin is corrupted by the easy-believism that omits it altogether, offering a decision without any sense of guilt, and by the morbid scrupulosity that stops at conviction and never moves on to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant corruption of our age is easy-believism, which strips conviction of sin out of the gospel altogether. Sinners are urged to make a decision, say a prayer, or accept Christ without ever being brought to feel the weight of their guilt or the justice of their condemnation; sin is minimized, the law is muted, and the wrath of God against the sinner is left unmentioned for fear of giving offence. But the Spirit's appointed order is to reprove the world of sin (John 16:8), and the apostolic preaching pierced the heart and provoked the cry, "what shall we do?" (Acts 2:37). A faith that was never preceded by any sense of need has nothing to lay hold of in a Savior, for they that be whole need not a physician. The recovery of the doctrine requires the recovery of law-preaching: that men may know their guilt, despair of themselves, and so be driven to Christ. False peace is the great danger of an unconvicted profession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The opposite error, less common but real, is to make conviction an end in itself—a morbid, introspective dwelling on guilt that never rises to faith in Christ. Some souls, truly awakened, sink under the burden of sin and stay there, treating the depth of their sorrow as if it were a qualification for grace, when conviction is meant only to empty the hand that it may receive Christ. The positive biblical principle to recover is that conviction always aims beyond itself: it is the Spirit's plough, not His harvest; it breaks the ground that the gospel seed may take root. Therefore the convicted soul is to be pointed at once away from his sin and his sorrow alike, and toward the cross, where the blood of Christ cleanseth from all sin—for godly sorrow worketh repentance unto salvation, not to be repented of.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on Christ's promise that the Comforter would elenchō (reprove, convict) the world of sin (John 16:8), fastening guilt upon the conscience that the sinner may flee to Christ.
roots_lines: Greek elenchō (G1651) — to convict, reprove, expose; the verb of John 16:8, the Spirit convicting the world of sin.
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, correct, decide; the Old Testament background of the Spirit's reproving work.
Greek katanyssō (G2660) — to prick sharply, pierce; the verb of Acts 2:37, the hearers pricked in heart.
Greek lype (G3077) — sorrow, grief; the godly sorrow that worketh repentance unto salvation (2 Cor 7:10).
Conviction is the Spirit's plough, preparatory and ongoing, ever aiming beyond itself at the cross of Christ.
usage: Under the preaching of the law, deep Conviction of Sin laid hold of him, and he cried out, like Peter's hearers, "what shall I do?"
Easy-believism dispenses with Conviction of Sin, offering a Savior to those who have never felt themselves lost.
Conviction of Sin is the Spirit's plough, not His harvest—it breaks the heart only that the gospel seed may take root in Christ.

etymology: From Latin conformare, to fashion after a pattern; rendering the Greek symmorphos, having the same form, in Paul's "predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Rom 8:29).
biblical_def: Conformity to Christ is the appointed end of sanctification: the gracious work of God whereby the elect are increasingly fashioned after the likeness of the Lord Jesus in holiness, until at the last they are made perfectly like Him. The charter text is Romans 8:29: "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren." The word is symmorphos, sharing the same form—not a mere outward imitation, but an inward refashioning of the whole man after the pattern of Christ. This conformity is comprehended within the golden chain of redemption: those whom God foreknew He predestined, and the very thing He predestined them to is Christlikeness. It is therefore certain of accomplishment, for the same God who called and justified will also glorify. The process is progressive in this life—"we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory" (2 Cor 3:18)—and perfect at the last, for "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). It must be sharply distinguished from the therapeutic self-actualization of the age, which makes the goal of life the realizing of one's own potential, the becoming of one's "best self," the flourishing of the autonomous individual. The Christian's goal is not self-actualization but Christ-conformity; not the expression of the self but the crucifixion of the old self and the putting on of Christ. The image to which he is being conformed is not within him to be drawn out, but in Christ to be impressed upon him by the Spirit through the means of grace. This dictionary confesses conformity to the image of God's Son as the fixed and certain end for which the elect were chosen, the substance of their sanctification, and their consummation in glory.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONFORMITY as likeness; correspondence in form, manner, or character; compliance with a pattern. Conformity to Christ is the work of God fashioning the elect after the image of His Son (Rom 8:29).
webster_full: CONFORMITY, n. — 1. Likeness; correspondence with a model in form or manner; resemblance; agreement; congruity. 2. Consistency; agreement; as conformity of life to doctrine.
In the spiritual sense, Conformity to Christ is the predestined refashioning of the believer after the image of the Son of God in holiness.
"Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Rom 8:29).
It requires the inward refashioning of the whole man after the pattern of Christ; it forbids mistaking the goal for therapeutic self-actualization.
It is progressive now—changed from glory to glory—and perfect at the last, when the saints shall see Him and be made like Him.
scriptures: For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you.
corruption_summary: Conformity to Christ is corrupted when the goal of the Christian life is exchanged for therapeutic self-actualization—the realizing of one's potential and the flourishing of the autonomous self—rather than the crucifying of the old self and the putting on of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the therapeutic gospel, which quietly substitutes self-actualization for conformity to Christ. The self becomes the center: the aim of life is to become one's "best self," to realize one's potential, to flourish, to be authentic, to express the identity supposed to lie within. Even churches preach a Christ who helps the listener become the man he always wanted to be, baptizing the autonomous self's ambitions with religious language. But Scripture sets a different end: not the expression of the self but its crucifixion—"I am crucified with Christ"—and the putting on of a new man created after Christ. The image to which the believer is conformed is not latent within him to be drawn out, but is in Christ, to be impressed upon him by the Spirit. The remedy is to recover the biblical telos: Christlikeness, holiness, the death of self-will, and the bearing of the image of the Son.

A subtler form of the same error infects much spiritual-formation and discipleship language, where techniques and practices are commended for their power to make one calmer, more whole, more fulfilled—the benefits accruing to the self rather than the glory accruing to Christ. Even sanctification can be marketed as self-improvement. The recovery is to remember that conformity to Christ is not therapy and not self-help, but the predestined work of God fashioning the elect after His Son (Rom 8:29), worked by the Spirit through the ordinary means of grace, and aiming not at the comfort of the self but at the glory of Christ, that He might be the firstborn among many brethren. The Christian is being made, not into a better version of himself, but into the likeness of his Lord.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on Paul's symmorphous tēs eikonos tou huiou autou (Rom 8:29), conformity to the image of the Son, the predestined end of the elect, perfected in glory.
roots_lines: Greek symmorphos (G4832) — conformed, sharing the same form; the inward refashioning of the believer after Christ (Rom 8:29).
Greek eikōn (G1504) — image, likeness; Christ as the image of God, after which the saints are fashioned.
Greek metamorphoō (G3339) — to transform, transfigure; the verb of 2 Cor 3:18, changed from glory to glory.
Greek morphoō (G3445) — to form; Paul travailing until Christ be formed in the Galatians (Gal 4:19).
The goal is Christlikeness, not self-actualization—the crucifying of the old self and the putting on of the new after the image of God's Son.
usage: The end of sanctification is not personal fulfillment but Conformity to Christ, fashioning the believer after the image of God's Son.
He learned that the gospel calls not for self-actualization but for Conformity to Christ—the death of self-will and the putting on of the Savior.
Conformity to Christ is progressive now and perfect hereafter, when the saints shall see Him and be made like Him.

etymology: From the Greek ho palaios anthrōpos (the old man) and ho kainos anthrōpos (the new man) of Eph 4:22-24; man here denoting the whole person in his fallen or renewed condition.
biblical_def: The Old Man and the New Man are Paul's paired figures for the believer's former condition in Adam and his renewed condition in Christ—the whole self as it was, corrupt and under sin, and the whole self as it is being made, righteous and holy. The texts are Ephesians 4:22-24: "That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; And be renewed in the spirit of your mind; And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness"; and Colossians 3:9-10: "ye have put off the old man with his deeds; And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him." The decisive declaration is Romans 6:6: "Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin." The doctrine holds together a definitive and a progressive truth, and to sever them is to err. Definitively, in union with Christ the old man has already been crucified—the reign of sin is broken, the dominion overthrown, the believer no longer a slave of sin but now in principle a new creation; this is an accomplished fact stated in the aorist, not a goal to be attained. Progressively, on the ground of that accomplished fact, the believer is commanded daily to put off the old man with his deeds and to put on the new—to reckon himself dead indeed unto sin but alive unto God, mortifying the remaining corruptions and quickening the graces of the renewed nature. The new man is "created in righteousness and true holiness," after the image of God, so that the goal is again conformity to Christ. The two aspects are not two contradictory teachings but the indicative and the imperative of the gospel: be what you are. This dictionary confesses that the old man is crucified once for all in Christ, and that the believer, on that very ground, is to put off the old and put on the new throughout his pilgrimage, until the new man is perfected in glory.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 treats MAN as a human being, and figuratively the moral nature or condition. The Old Man / New Man are Paul's figures for the believer's former corrupt self in Adam and his renewed self in Christ (Eph 4:22-24).
webster_full: MAN, n. — A human being; mankind; the human race. Figuratively, the moral nature or condition of a person; the inward man, the natural man, the spiritual man.
In the spiritual sense, the Old Man is the believer's former corrupt condition in Adam, and the New Man his renewed condition in Christ.
"Put off... the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts... and put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" (Eph 4:22-24).
It requires that we reckon the old man crucified with Christ and daily put off his deeds; it forbids severing the definitive fact from the progressive command.
The old man is crucified once for all (Rom 6:6); the new man, created after the image of God, is to be put on and perfected unto glory.
scriptures: That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; And be renewed in the spirit of your mind; And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds; And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him.
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
corruption_summary: The Old Man / New Man doctrine is corrupted when the definitive and progressive aspects are severed—either by an antinomian presumption that ignores the command to mortify, or by a striving that forgets the old man is already crucified in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The errors that beset this doctrine are perennial rather than novel, and both arise from severing the definitive from the progressive. The first is the antinomian presumption that, because the old man is crucified with Christ, the believer need give no diligence to put off his deeds—treating Romans 6:6 as if it abolished the command to mortify, when Paul draws the very opposite inference: therefore reckon yourselves dead unto sin and yield not your members unto unrighteousness. The positive principle to recover is that the indicative grounds the imperative; the old man is crucified that we should not serve sin, and the broken reign of sin is the basis, not the abolition, of the daily putting off.

The second error is the opposite striving that forgets the accomplished fact—the believer who labors to crucify the old man by his own effort, as though the dominion of sin were still unbroken and the outcome of the warfare doubtful, sinking into bondage and despair. The recovery here is to rest on the finished work: the old man is crucified, the body of sin is destroyed in principle, the believer is a new creature in Christ (2 Cor 5:17). On that settled ground he fights, not for victory but from victory, putting off the old and putting on the new, renewed in the spirit of his mind, after the image of Him that created him. Definitive and progressive belong together: be what you are. To recover the doctrine is to hold both, never resting in the indicative so as to neglect the imperative, never straining at the imperative so as to forget the indicative.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on Paul's palaios anthrōpos (old man) and kainos anthrōpos (new man) of Eph 4:22-24 and Col 3:9-10, with the old man crucified with Christ in Rom 6:6.
roots_lines: Greek palaios (G3820) — old, former, worn-out; the old man, the believer's former corrupt condition in Adam.
Greek kainos (G2537) — new in kind, fresh; the new man, created after God in righteousness and true holiness.
Greek anthrōpos (G444) — man, human being; here the whole person in his fallen or renewed condition.
Greek systauroō (G4957) — to crucify together with; the old man crucified with Christ in Rom 6:6.
The figure holds the definitive (the old man crucified once for all) and the progressive (the daily putting off and putting on) together as indicative and imperative.
usage: Because the Old Man is already crucified with Christ, the believer fights remaining sin from victory, not for it.
Paul bids the saints put off the Old Man with his deeds and put on the New Man, created after God in righteousness and true holiness.
To sever the definitive from the progressive in the Old Man / New Man doctrine breeds either antinomian presumption or despairing self-effort.

etymology: From Paul's charge to Timothy, anazopyrein to charisma, to rekindle into flame the gift; Greek anazopyreō (to fan into flame) and charisma (gift of grace), in 2 Tim 1:6.
biblical_def: To Stir Up the Gift is the apostolic charge laid upon the minister to kindle, exercise, and diligently improve the spiritual gift God has bestowed on him for his office. Paul writes to Timothy: "Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands" (2 Tim 1:6). The verb is anazopyreō, to fan a fire into fresh flame—a vivid figure: the gift is like coals which, though never extinguished, may grow dim and sluggish through neglect, and must be stirred and blown upon that they may blaze again. The charisma here is the ministerial gifting conferred upon Timothy for the work of the evangelist and pastor, attested by the laying on of the presbytery's hands (1 Tim 4:14), comprehending the abilities for preaching, teaching, and oversight. The charge implies two truths. First, the gift is God's gift, sovereignly bestowed; the minister does not generate it but receives it. Second, the gift is given to be used, and the responsibility to employ it diligently rests upon the man who has it. Paul therefore presses the same point: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee" (1 Tim 4:14), and "give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine... meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them" (1 Tim 4:13, 15). The charge stands against ministerial sloth, that besetting sin which lets gifts lie buried like the wicked servant's talent, that grows cold in study, slack in prayer, and perfunctory in preaching. As cessationist, this dictionary does not regard the gift in view as a continuing sign-gift such as tongues or healing, but as the abiding gifts of teaching, exhortation, and rule that Christ still gives His church through her ministers. This dictionary confesses that every man entrusted with a gift for Christ's service is bound to stir it up, to fan it into flame by diligent use, prayer, and meditation, lest by sloth he bury what God has given for the good of His people.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines to STIR UP as to incite, instigate, or rouse to action; and GIFT as a present or endowment bestowed. To Stir Up the Gift is to rouse and diligently exercise the ministerial gifting God has bestowed (2 Tim 1:6).
webster_full: STIR, v.t. — To excite; to instigate; to prompt; to rouse into action; as, to stir up the embers of a fire, or to stir up the mind.
GIFT, n. — A present; a thing given or bestowed; the act of giving; the right or power of giving; also, the faculty or power bestowed; an endowment.
"Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands" (2 Tim 1:6).
It requires the diligent kindling and exercise of the gift through study, prayer, and use; it forbids the sloth and neglect that lets the gift grow cold and dim.
The gift is God's sovereign bestowal, yet given to be improved—the minister must fan it into flame lest he bury it like the wicked servant's talent.
scriptures: Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.
And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine.
corruption_summary: The charge to Stir Up the Gift confronts ministerial sloth and neglect—the burying of God-given gifts through coldness in study, prayer, and labor—and warns against presuming on a gift while failing to exercise it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger this charge addresses is not a modern redefinition but the perennial sin of sloth in the Lord's servants. The man entrusted with a gift for Christ's service may, through ease, discouragement, or the press of lesser things, let his gift grow dim—coals that smoulder for want of stirring. His study grows shallow, his prayers brief, his preaching mechanical, until the gift that once blazed gives little light or heat. Against this Paul charges Timothy to fan the gift into flame (2 Tim 1:6) and to neglect it not (1 Tim 4:14). The positive principle to recover is diligent improvement: the minister is bound to give attendance to reading, exhortation, and doctrine, to meditate upon these things and give himself wholly to them, that his profiting may appear to all.

A related abuse is presumption upon the gift without its exercise—the man who, conscious of real ability, trusts the gift to carry him and so labors little, neglecting the means by which the gift is kept bright. But gifts unimproved are gifts despised, and the parable of the talents warns that the servant who buries what his lord entrusted is called wicked and slothful, and what he has is taken from him (Matt 25:25-29). The recovery is to hold gift and diligence together: the gift is God's, freely given and not earned; yet it is given to be used, and the steward is accountable to improve it with all diligence, prayer, and labor, for the good of the church and the glory of the Giver. To stir up the gift is no optional fervor but a binding charge upon all whom Christ has gifted for His service.
roots_summary: The charge rests on Paul's anazopyrein to charisma tou theou (2 Tim 1:6), to fan into flame the gift of God—the diligent kindling of ministerial gifting against sloth.
roots_lines: Greek anazopyreō (G329) — to rekindle, fan into flame; the vivid verb of 2 Tim 1:6, the gift stirred like coals into fresh fire.
Greek charisma (G5486) — gift of grace; the ministerial endowment God bestows for the work of His service.
Greek ameleō (G272) — to neglect, be careless of; the verb forbidden in 1 Tim 4:14, "neglect not the gift."
Greek meletō (G3191) — to meditate, attend to, practise; the diligent attendance commanded in 1 Tim 4:15.
The gift is God's sovereign bestowal, yet given to be improved, and the steward is bound to fan it into flame by diligent use.
usage: Paul charged Timothy to Stir Up the Gift of God that was in him, lest it grow cold through neglect.
Wearied by long labor, the old pastor resolved afresh to Stir Up the Gift, giving himself wholly to reading, prayer, and doctrine.
To Stir Up the Gift is no optional fervor but a binding charge against the sloth that buries what God has given.

etymology: From Latin examinare, to weigh, test, try; rendering the Greek peirazō and dokimazō in Paul's "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" (2 Cor 13:5).
biblical_def: Self-Examination is the duty whereby a Christian honestly tries his own heart, faith, and life before God, to discern whether he be truly in the faith and to detect and mortify his besetting sins. Paul commands it directly: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" (2 Cor 13:5). The verbs are peirazō and dokimazō, to test and to prove as metal is assayed for its genuineness. A particular and solemn occasion of this duty is the approach to the Lord's table: "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup" (1 Cor 11:28), lest he eat and drink unworthily and bring judgment on himself. The Puritans were masters of this exercise, urging the saints to spread their hearts open before the all-seeing God, to compare their state with the marks of grace the word lays down—love of the brethren, hatred of sin, delight in God's law, the keeping of His commandments—and so to make their calling and election sure. Self-examination has two great uses: it confirms the assurance of the sincere, who upon trial find the evidences of grace; and it disturbs the false peace of the hypocrite and the formalist, who upon trial find nothing of Christ within. Yet it must be carefully distinguished from a morbid, anxious introspection that turns the soul perpetually inward upon itself, breeds doubt and despair, and never lifts the eye to Christ. Healthy self-examination always issues in fresh recourse to the Savior—searching the heart that one may flee anew to the blood that cleanseth, not that one may rest in the search. This dictionary confesses self-examination as a necessary and wholesome duty of the Christian, commanded in the word, practised before the Supper, aimed at the trial of one's faith and the mortification of sin, and ever ending not in self but in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EXAMINATION as the act of examining; a careful search or inquiry with a view to discover truth. Self-Examination is the believer's honest trying of his own heart, faith, and life before God (2 Cor 13:5).
webster_full: EXAMINATION, n. — The act of examining; a careful search or inquiry with a view to discover truth; the act of viewing or considering; inquiry into facts or principles by interrogatories.
SELF-EXAMINATION, n. — An examination into one's own state, conduct, and motives, particularly in regard to religious feelings and duties.
"Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" (2 Cor 13:5).
It requires the honest trial of one's faith by the marks of grace in the word, especially before the Lord's Supper; it forbids the morbid introspection that never looks to Christ.
It confirms the assurance of the sincere and disturbs the false peace of the hypocrite—ever ending not in self, but in Christ.
scriptures: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.
Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.
corruption_summary: Self-Examination is corrupted on one side by the neglect that lets men live in false peace untried, and on the other by a morbid, anxious introspection that turns the soul perpetually inward and never flees to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruptions of this duty are the old ones. The first is simple neglect—the unexamined profession that takes its own salvation for granted, never tries itself by the marks of grace, and so rests in a false peace that the day of judgment will shatter. Against this Paul commands, "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2 Cor 13:5), and warns that a man may approach the Lord's table unworthily, eating and drinking judgment to himself, for want of self-trial (1 Cor 11:28-29). The positive principle to recover is the wholesome Puritan practice of trying one's heart honestly before the all-seeing God—"Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Ps 139:23)—comparing one's state with the evidences of true grace the word describes, that the calling and election may be made sure.

The opposite corruption is morbid introspection—an endless, anxious turning of the eye inward that breeds scrupulosity, doubt, and despair, dissecting every motive until the soul is paralyzed and Christ is lost from view. This is not the self-examination Scripture commands but a snare of the enemy, who, if he cannot keep a man careless, will make him morbidly self-occupied. The recovery is to mark the proper end of the duty: self-examination is never an end in itself and never terminates upon the self. Its purpose is to drive the soul afresh to Christ—to find sin that one may mortify it, to find grace that one may bless God for it, and in either case to flee anew to the Savior. Healthy trial of the heart always ends with the eye lifted off self and fixed upon the blood that cleanseth from all sin.
roots_summary: The duty rests on Paul's heautous peirazete... dokimazete (2 Cor 13:5), the trying and proving of one's own self in the faith, and the self-examination before the Supper (1 Cor 11:28).
roots_lines: Greek peirazō (G3985) — to test, try, prove; "examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2 Cor 13:5).
Greek dokimazō (G1381) — to prove, assay as metal; "prove your own selves," testing for genuineness.
Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, examine; "search me, O God, and know my heart" (Ps 139:23).
Hebrew chaphas (H2664) — to search diligently; "let us search and try our ways" (Lam 3:40).
The trial is the honest weighing of heart and life by the word, ever ending not in self but in Christ.
usage: Before coming to the Lord's table, the godly man practised Self-Examination, trying his heart honestly before God.
Paul's command, "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith," binds every professor to Self-Examination.
True Self-Examination is no morbid introspection; it tries the heart only to drive the soul afresh to Christ.

etymology: From the figure of Hebrews 6:19, hope as ankyran tēs psychēs, an anchor of the soul; Greek ankyra (anchor) and psychē (soul), borrowed from the seaman's steadying gear.
biblical_def: The Anchor of the Soul is the scriptural figure for the Christian's hope, set forth in Hebrews 6:19: "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil." As an anchor steadies a ship against wind and tide, holding her fast amid storm, so the believer's hope steadies the soul against the tempests of affliction, doubt, and temptation, keeping it from being driven and tossed. But the figure is heightened in a wonderful way: this anchor is cast not downward into the shifting seabed below, but upward and inward, "into that within the veil"—into the very holy of holies in heaven, where Jesus the forerunner is for us entered (Heb 6:20). The believer's hope is moored to Christ Himself, seated at the right hand of God within the heavenly sanctuary; the cable runs from the storm-tossed soul on earth to the immovable Savior in glory. The ground of this hope's sureness is twofold: the immutable promise of God and His oath, "two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie" (Heb 6:18), and the entrance of Christ as forerunner, who has gone before to secure the harbor and bring His people safely in. Thus the anchor is "sure and stedfast"—sure in itself, fastened in heaven, and steadfast in its hold, never to drag or slip. This figure undergirds the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints: because the anchor is fixed in Christ within the veil, and not in the believer's own strength, the soul cannot finally be carried away; the same Lord who is the object of the hope is the keeper of the soul that hopes. This dictionary confesses that the believer's hope, grounded in God's oath and moored to the ascended Christ within the veil, is a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, the very ground of his perseverance unto the end.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ANCHOR as an iron instrument for holding a ship at rest in water, and figuratively that which gives stability or security. The Anchor of the Soul is the believer's hope, sure and steadfast, moored to Christ within the veil (Heb 6:19).
webster_full: ANCHOR, n. — An iron instrument for holding a ship or other vessel at rest in water. Figuratively, that which gives stability or security; that on which we place dependence for safety.
In the spiritual sense, the Anchor of the Soul is the Christian's hope, fastened not in the shifting seabed but in heaven, where Christ the forerunner is entered.
"Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil" (Heb 6:19).
It requires that hope be moored to the ascended Christ and grounded on God's oath; it forbids resting the soul's security on its own strength or feelings.
Being sure and steadfast, the anchor cannot drag or slip—it is the very ground of the believer's perseverance unto the end.
scriptures: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil.
That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us.
Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.
And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.
corruption_summary: The Anchor of the Soul faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is a sure, objective hope moored to the ascended Christ, against the modern reduction of hope to mere optimism or wishful sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The figure of the anchor stands clear of the culture-war controversies, yet the biblical hope it pictures is widely diluted in modern usage, where "hope" has shrunk to mean a vague optimism, a hopeful feeling, a wish that things may turn out well. So weakened, hope becomes a sentiment as shifting as the sea it is meant to weather, anchored to nothing, holding nothing fast. The positive principle to recover is the objective and sure character of biblical hope: it is not a feeling that the believer generates but a confident expectation grounded on the immutable promise and oath of God, in which it is impossible for Him to lie (Heb 6:18). Hope, biblically, is as certain as the God on whose word it rests.

The greater recovery is the direction and ground of the anchor. The believer's hope is moored not in himself, nor in his circumstances, nor in the visible and shifting things of earth, but "within the veil," in the heavenly sanctuary where Christ the forerunner is entered (Heb 6:19-20). Because the cable runs from the storm-tossed soul to the immovable Savior in glory, the anchor is sure and steadfast and cannot finally slip. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints: the soul is kept, not by the firmness of its own grip, but by the fixedness of the anchor in Christ. To recover the doctrine is to teach the trembling believer to look away from his own wavering frame to the steadfast object of his hope, and to find his soul held fast by the One who has gone before within the veil.
roots_summary: The figure rests on the ankyra tēs psychēs of Heb 6:19, hope as an anchor sure and steadfast, entering within the veil where Christ the forerunner is gone before.
roots_lines: Greek ankyra (G45) — anchor; the seaman's steadying gear, here the figure of the believer's hope (Heb 6:19).
Greek psychē (G5590) — soul, life; the soul steadied by hope amid the storms of affliction.
Greek elpis (G1680) — hope; the confident expectation grounded on God's oath, not a mere wish.
Greek prodromos (G4274) — forerunner; Christ entered within the veil to secure the harbor for His people (Heb 6:20).
The anchor is moored not below but above, within the veil, fixed in the ascended Christ—the ground of the saints' perseverance.
usage: When the storms of affliction beat upon him, his hope held him fast, the Anchor of the Soul, sure and steadfast.
The Anchor of the Soul is cast not into the shifting seabed but within the veil, moored to the ascended Christ.
Because the Anchor of the Soul is fixed in Christ and not in the believer's own strength, the saints cannot finally be carried away.

etymology: From Peter's sermon, kairoi anapsyxeōs, seasons of refreshing, in Acts 3:19; Greek anapsyxis (a recovery of breath, refreshment) from anapsychō, to cool again, revive.
biblical_def: Times of Refreshing are the seasons of spiritual reviving, comfort, and rest that come to the people of God from His own presence. Peter preaches: "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord" (Acts 3:19). The word is anapsyxis, a cooling again, a catching of breath, a relief—the figure of one spent and panting who is revived. The phrase looks chiefly to the consolations the Lord grants His people in this life as the fruit of repentance and conversion: seasons when His presence is sweetly near, when the burdens of guilt are eased by fresh sense of pardon, when the soul, weary and faint, is quickened and revived by the Spirit through the word and the means of grace. Some refer the words also to the consummate refreshing at the return of Christ, when the saints enter their eternal rest; both senses honor the truth that refreshment flows wholly from the presence of the Lord, not from any source in the creature. The Scriptures speak often of this mutual refreshing among the saints: Philemon's love had refreshed the bowels of the saints (Phm 7), and the coming of Stephanas and his companions "refreshed my spirit and yours" (1 Cor 16:18), so that the Lord ordinarily conveys His reviving not only directly but through the fellowship and kindness of His people. This refreshment must be carefully distinguished from the worked-up excitement of the revival-bench and from the modern craving for emotional experience; true reviving comes from the presence of the Lord, is wrought by His Spirit through His appointed means, issues in repentance and holiness, and bows the soul down before God rather than puffing it up. This dictionary confesses that the Lord grants His weary people real seasons of spiritual refreshing—rest, comfort, and reviving from His own presence—ever flowing from grace and tending unto holiness, and consummated in the everlasting rest that remaineth for the people of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REFRESHING as the act of reviving from heat or fatigue; that which gives fresh strength or vigor. Times of Refreshing are the seasons of spiritual reviving and rest that come from the presence of the Lord (Acts 3:19).
webster_full: REFRESH, v.t. — To revive; to reanimate after depression; to give new strength to; to relieve after fatigue; as, sleep refreshes the body and the mind.
In the spiritual sense, Times of Refreshing are the seasons of reviving, comfort, and rest that the Lord grants His weary people from His own presence.
"Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord" (Acts 3:19).

It requires that true reviving be sought from the presence of the Lord through His appointed means, issuing in repentance and holiness; it forbids the worked-up excitement that mistakes emotion for the Spirit.
The Lord refreshes His people directly by His Spirit, and also through the love and fellowship of the saints (Phm 7; 1 Cor 16:18).
scriptures: Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord.
For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother.
For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Times of Refreshing are corrupted when spiritual reviving is reduced to worked-up emotional excitement sought for its own sake, rather than the rest and comfort that come from the presence of the Lord and issue in repentance and holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption is the reduction of true reviving to manufactured emotional experience. Whole methods have arisen, from the revival-bench to the modern stage, designed to produce the feelings of refreshing—a wave of emotion, a sense of release, a thrill of presence—by music, atmosphere, and technique, and to treat the intensity of the feeling as the measure of the Spirit's working. But Peter says the times of refreshing come "from the presence of the Lord" (Acts 3:19), not from the contrivances of men, and they come in the way of repentance and conversion, not as a substitute for them. A refreshing that leaves a man unrepentant, unholy, and unhumbled is no refreshing from God, however moving the experience. The recovery is to seek reviving where God has promised it: in His presence, through His word, sacraments, and prayer, in the path of repentance and faith.

A subtler corruption craves the experience of refreshing as an end in itself—the spiritually restless soul that runs from meeting to meeting and book to book seeking the next quickening, hungry for the feeling rather than for the Lord whose presence gives it. But the rest Christ offers is found in coming to Him: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28). The positive principle to recover is that refreshment is a fruit of grace and a gift of God's presence, ever tending unto holiness, and that its consummation is the everlasting rest which remaineth for the people of God. The Lord refreshes His weary people—directly by His Spirit, and through the love and fellowship of the saints, whose kindness refreshes the bowels of the brethren (Phm 7; 1 Cor 16:18)—that they may be revived to serve Him, not merely to feel revived.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on Peter's kairoi anapsyxeōs apo prosōpou tou kyriou (Acts 3:19), seasons of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, with the mutual refreshing of the saints (Phm 7; 1 Cor 16:18).
roots_lines: Greek anapsyxis (G403) — a recovery of breath, refreshment, revival; the seasons of refreshing in Acts 3:19.
Greek anapsychō (G404) — to cool again, revive, refresh; the verb behind the figure of reviving the weary.
Greek anapauō (G373) — to give rest, refresh; the rest Christ gives the heavy laden (Matt 11:28) and the saints refreshed (Phm 7).
Greek kairos (G2540) — season, appointed time; the seasons in which the Lord grants His reviving.
True refreshing flows from the presence of the Lord through His appointed means, issuing in repentance and holiness, not from worked-up emotion.
usage: After long heaviness, the Lord granted him Times of Refreshing, reviving his weary soul by the word and sweet sense of pardon.
Times of Refreshing come from the presence of the Lord, not from the contrivances of the revival-bench.
The kindness of the brethren refreshed his spirit, for the Lord conveys His Times of Refreshing also through the fellowship of the saints.
